noun:April.tx: Inherited from Middle High German aberelle.

prep:ab.tx: From Middle High German abe, ab, from Old High German ab, from Proto-West Germanic *ab, from Proto-Germanic *ab.

adj:ab.tx: From adverbial use of the prefix ab- in verbs such as abschlagen, abgehen etc. Compare English off.

adj:abnormal.tx: Related to Latin ab- and normal

adj:abstinent.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin abstinēns, 16th century.

conj:also.tx: From Middle High German alles, from Old High German also, alsō (“as, like”); equivalent to all + so. Cognate with English also, as.

adv:also.tx: From Middle High German alles, from Old High German also, alsō (“as, like”); equivalent to all + so. Cognate with English also, as.

intj:also.tx: From Middle High German alles, from Old High German also, alsō (“as, like”); equivalent to all + so. Cognate with English also, as.

prep:after.tx: From Middle High German after, from Old High German after.

prep:an.tx: From Middle High German an(e), from Old High German ana, from Proto-West Germanic *ana, from Proto-Germanic *ana.

adv:an.tx: From Middle High German an(e), from Old High German ana, from Proto-West Germanic *ana, from Proto-Germanic *ana.

adj:an.tx: From Middle High German an(e), from Old High German ana, from Proto-West Germanic *ana, from Proto-Germanic *ana.

det:all.tx: From Middle High German al, from Old High German al, from Proto-West Germanic *all, from Proto-Germanic *allaz.

adj:arm.tx: From Middle High German arm, from Old High German arm, from Proto-West Germanic *arm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erH- (“to be sparse”) or alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ-, whence English orphan. Cognate with Old English earm.

adj:ambivalent.tx: From ambi-, ambo and valens (inflected valent-), valeo.

noun:Apfel.tx: From Middle High German apfel, from Old High German apful, from Proto-West Germanic *applu, from Proto-Germanic *apluz (compare Dutch appel, West Frisian apel, English apple), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ébōl.

adj:astral.tx: From Late Latin astralis, from Latin astrum (“star”) + -ālis, the first element from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”).

intj:ah.tx: From Middle High German ā, from Old High German a, ah, from Proto-West Germanic *a, *ah. Cognate with Middle Low German a, Middle English a, aa, ah (whence English ah).

num:acht.tx: From Middle High German ahte, from Old High German ahto, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtō, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōu, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Compare Dutch acht, English eight, Danish otte, Swedish åtta, Greek οκτώ (októ), Latin octō.

intj:ach.tx: From Middle High German ach, from Old High German ah.

noun:Abteilung.tx: From Middle High German abteilunge. Equivalent to abteilen + -ung.

noun:Affe.tx: From Middle High German affe, from Old High German affo, from Proto-West Germanic *apō, from Proto-Germanic *apô. The sense of drunkenness has been traced to the late 18ᵗʰ century, allegedly playing on the homophony of Czech opice (“monkey or ape”) and opít se (“to get drunk”), though the image of a monkey being a possessing demon is translingual, and thus Spanish mona (“she-monkey”) also means …

prep:auf.tx: From Middle High German ūf, from Old High German ūf, from Proto-Germanic *upp. This form with a lengthened vowel is originally Upper German. Central German forms were Middle High German uf and (western) up. Compare Dutch op, Low German op, Luxembourgish op, English up.

adj:auf.tx: From Middle High German ūf, from Old High German ūf, from Proto-Germanic *upp. This form with a lengthened vowel is originally Upper German. Central German forms were Middle High German uf and (western) up. Compare Dutch op, Low German op, Luxembourgish op, English up.

adv:auf.tx: From Middle High German ūf, from Old High German ūf, from Proto-Germanic *upp. This form with a lengthened vowel is originally Upper German. Central German forms were Middle High German uf and (western) up. Compare Dutch op, Low German op, Luxembourgish op, English up.

intj:auf.tx: From Middle High German ūf, from Old High German ūf, from Proto-Germanic *upp. This form with a lengthened vowel is originally Upper German. Central German forms were Middle High German uf and (western) up. Compare Dutch op, Low German op, Luxembourgish op, English up.

adj:aper.tx: From Middle High German āber, from Old High German ābar (“sunny, warm, dry”), from ā- (“from, away”, prefix) + bar (“bare”), likely via a defunct verb *ābarēn, *ābarōn (“to lay bare, expose”). Alternatively, from a verb *āberan (“to not bear, not carry”). Sense likely influenced by unrelated Latin aprīcus due to superficial similarity of form and meaning.

noun:Arzt.tx: From Middle High German arzet, arzāt, from Old High German arzāt, from Latin archīāter (“physician”), from Ancient Greek ἀρχῐᾱτρός (arkhĭātrós), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + ἰατρός (iatrós).

noun:Ärztin.tx: From Middle High German arzātīn, arzātinne. Equivalent to Arzt + -in, with umlaut.

noun:Asche.tx: From Middle High German asche, from Old High German asca, from Proto-West Germanic *askā, from Proto-Germanic *askǭ. Compare Low German Asch, Dutch as, English ash, Danish aske, Swedish aska.

verb:arbeiten.tx: From Old High German arbeiten, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidijaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”), from which English orphan is also derived. Cognates include Dutch arbeiden, Old Saxon arvedian, Gothic 𐌰𐍂𐌱𐌰𐌹𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (arbaidjan).

conj:aber.tx: From Middle High German aber, aver, from Old High German aber, ābar, abur, aver, avur, afur, from Proto-Germanic *aferą (“behind”). Compare Bavarian owa (“but”), Luxembourgish awer (“but”), Saterland Frisian oaber (“but”), Middle Low German āver, German Low German aver (“but”).

adv:aber.tx: From Middle High German aber, aver, from Old High German aber, ābar, abur, aver, avur, afur, from Proto-Germanic *aferą (“behind”). Compare Bavarian owa (“but”), Luxembourgish awer (“but”), Saterland Frisian oaber (“but”), Middle Low German āver, German Low German aver (“but”).

noun:Auge.tx: From Middle High German ouge, from Old High German ouga, from Proto-West Germanic *augā, from Proto-Germanic *augô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Modern cognates include Alemannic German Aug, Bavarian Aug, Dutch oog, English eye, Icelandic auga, Swedish öga.

intj:amen.tx: Borrowed from Latin āmēn, from Ancient Greek ἀμήν (amḗn), from Hebrew אמן.

noun:Apache.tx: From Spanish apache, likely in part through English Apache. Further origin uncertain; possibly from Zuni ˀa˙paču.

adj:apart.tx: 16th century, from Middle French à part (“separately”). The modern sense follows the French attributive use as in une chose à part (“something of its kind, something exceptional”).

adj:average.tx: Borrowed from English average. Doublet of Havarie.

noun:Aufzug.tx: From Middle High German ūfzuc, verbal noun of ūfziehen.

adv:aus.tx: From Middle High German ūȥ, from Old High German ūȥ (“out”) from Proto-West Germanic *ūt. Compare Dutch uit, Low German ut, English out, Danish ud. Doublet of out.

adj:aus.tx: From Middle High German ūȥ, from Old High German ūȥ (“out”) from Proto-West Germanic *ūt. Compare Dutch uit, Low German ut, English out, Danish ud. Doublet of out.

prep:aus.tx: From Middle High German ūȥ, from Old High German ūȥ (“out”) from Proto-West Germanic *ūt. Compare Dutch uit, Low German ut, English out, Danish ud. Doublet of out.

noun:Adler.tx: From Middle High German adler, adelar, adelare, equivalent to edel (“noble”) + Aar (“eagle”). When Aar started assuming a more general meaning of "bird of prey suitable for hunting or falconry", the term Adelaar (edler Aar) emerged to distinguish eagles from other hunting birds such as falcons and hawks.

adv:anno.tx: Borrowed from Latin annō, ablative of annus. Compare Dutch anno.

adj:absolut.tx: 16th century, learned borrowing from Latin absolūtus, semantically influenced also by French absolu. The word became popular later on and widely entered the traditional dialects; compare e.g. Westphalian Low German abschluut.

adv:absolut.tx: 16th century, learned borrowing from Latin absolūtus, semantically influenced also by French absolu. The word became popular later on and widely entered the traditional dialects; compare e.g. Westphalian Low German abschluut.

noun:Achtung.tx: From Middle High German ahtunge (“consideration, appreciation”), from Old High German ahtunga, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtungu. By surface analysis, achten + -ung. Compare Yiddish אַכטונג (akhtung), Alemannic German Achtig.

intj:Achtung.tx: From Middle High German ahtunge (“consideration, appreciation”), from Old High German ahtunga, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtungu. By surface analysis, achten + -ung. Compare Yiddish אַכטונג (akhtung), Alemannic German Achtig.

adj:anonym.tx: Borrowed from French anonyme (adjective), from Latin anōnymus (adjective), from Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, adjective). By surface analysis, an- + -onym.

noun:Amaryllis.tx: From Latin Amaryllis (“a country girl in Virgil's Eclogues”), from Ancient Greek Ἀμαρυλλίς (Amarullís, from ἀμαρύσσω (amarússō, “to shine”)).

verb:auswachsen.tx: From aus- (“out”) + wachsen (“grow”). Compare Dutch uitwassen.

verb:aufstehen.tx: From auf- + stehen. Compare with Dutch opstaan and English stand up.

adj:alt.tx: From Middle High German alt, from Old High German alt, from Proto-West Germanic *ald, from Proto-Germanic *aldaz, from Proto-Indo-European *altós, *h₂eltós, from *h₂el- (“grow, nourish”). Compare Dutch oud, Low German old, West Frisian âld, English old. Doublet of Alt, a loanword from Italian.

noun:Arie.tx: Borrowed from Italian aria, from Latin āēr (“air (atmosphere), breath”).

adj:aktiv.tx: From Latin āctīvus, from agere (“to do, to act”).

noun:Aufmerksamkeit.tx: From aufmerksam + -keit. Cognate to Dutch opmerkzaamheid.

noun:Aussprache.tx: Deverbal from aussprechen, equivalent to aus- + Sprache.

noun:Armut.tx: From Middle High German armuot, armuote, from Old High German armuoti, from Proto-West Germanic *armōdī (“poverty”).

noun:Ansatz.tx: Back-formation from ansetzen. Equivalent to an- + Satz.

conj:als.tx: From Middle High German alles, from Old High German also, alsō (“as, like”); equivalent to all + so. Compare English as.

noun:Aal.tx: From Middle High German āl, from Old High German āl, from Proto-West Germanic *āl, whence English eel.

noun:Abakus.tx: Borrowed from Latin abacus, genitive and plural abacī.

noun:Abend.tx: From Middle High German ābent, from Old High German āband, from Proto-West Germanic *ābanþ, from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþs. Compare Low German Avend, Dutch avond, English eve, even (evening), Old Norse aptann, Swedish afton, Norwegian and Danish aften.

noun:Aberration.tx: From Latin aberrātiō, from aberrāre, equivalent to aberrieren + -ation.

noun:Abkürzung.tx: From abkürzen + -ung. Cognate with Swabian Abkirrzung, Alemannic German Abchörzig, Luxembourgish Ofkierzung.

noun:Abort.tx: Originally "remote place", at first in Middle Low German afort (16th century). The contemporary sense as a euphemism since the 18th century. Analysable as ab (“off, away”) + Ort (“place”).

noun:Absolvent.tx: Borrowed from Latin absolvēns, from absolvō (“to loosen from, to complete”).

noun:Abt.tx: From Middle High German abt, from Old High German abbat, borrowed from Late Latin abbas. Doublet of Abate.

noun:Acht.tx: Substantivation of the numeral acht (“eight”), from Old High German ahtô.

noun:Adel.tx: From Old High German adal, from Proto-West Germanic *aþal. More at athel. The surname is shortened from male given names beginning with Adel-.

noun:Adjutant.tx: 17th century, from Spanish ayudante, in part through French adjutant.

noun:Administrator.tx: Borrowed from Latin administrātor. The computing sense is a semantic loan from English.

noun:Admiral.tx: From English admiral, from Middle English, Anglo-Norman, and Old French admiral, from Medieval Latin admiralis, from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander”) + -alis (“-al”) under influence from admīrārī (“to admire, to respect”). Cognate with French amiral, etc.

noun:Advent.tx: From Middle High German advent, borrowed from Latin adventus.

noun:Aerobic.tx: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from aerobics. While aerobic exists in English to refer to aerobics, it is an adjective and not a noun.

noun:Afrikaner.tx: Possibly from Latin āfricānus + -er instead of -us

noun:After.tx: From Middle High German after, from Old High German aftero ("rear; behind; below"; compare Old High German aftar (“after”, preposition, adverb)), from Proto-Germanic *after, *aftiri (“more aft, further behind”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epóteros (“further behind, further away”), comparative form of *h₂epó (“off, behind”). Compare Dutch achter, Danish efter.

noun:Agar.tx: Borrowed from Malay agar or agar-agar, both meaning jelly.

noun:Agenda.tx: Borrowed from Latin agenda. Doublet of Agende.

noun:Agitation.tx: Borrowed from Latin agitātiō (“movement, action, agitation”).

noun:Agitator.tx: Borrowed from Latin agitātor (“driver”). Current meaning influenced by English agitator.

noun:Alarm.tx: Borrowed from Italian allarme. Cognate with French alarme. Doublet of Lärm.

noun:Algebra.tx: Borrowed from Latin algebra, from Arabic اَلْجَبْر (al-jabr), definite form of جَبْر (jabr).

noun:Alibi.tx: 18th century, from Latin alibī, chiefly through French alibi.

noun:All.tx: Substantivized neuter singular of the adjective all (“all”), without pronominal ending; from Proto-West Germanic *all, from Proto-Germanic *allaz. Present meaning “cosmos” from the 2nd half of the 17th century onwards.

noun:Alligator.tx: 16th century, in part directly from Spanish lagarto (“lizard”), in part through English alligator (and its variants). The contemporary form established itself during the 18th century following English (as in all European languages). Ultimately from Latin lacertus.

noun:Alt.tx: Borrowed from Italian alto from Latin altus. Doublet of alt.

noun:Altar.tx: From Middle High German alter, altære, from Old High German altāri, from Proto-West Germanic *altārī (“altar”), borrowed from Latin altāre. The form was readapted to the Latin source, partly to avoid homophony with Alter (“age”). Compare also Dutch altaar alongside archaic outer.

noun:Alter.tx: From Middle High German alter, from Old High German altar, from Proto-Germanic *aldrą. Cognate with German Low German Oller.

noun:Ambition.tx: Borrowed from French ambition, from Latin ambitiō.

noun:Ampere.tx: Named after the French physicist André-Marie Ampère.

noun:Amygdala.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin amygdala. Doublet of Mandel and Mandorla.

noun:Analysis.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin analysis. Doublet of Analyse (“analysis”, in a general sense).

noun:Ananas.tx: 16th century, from Middle French ananas and/or Dutch ananas, themselves from Portuguese ananás, from Old Tupi naná. In sense two, an abbreviation of Ananaserdbeere (literally “pineapple strawberry”), translating French fraise ananas.

noun:Anarchist.tx: Borrowed from French anarchiste, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía), from ἀν- (an-, “not, without”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “ruler”) + -ist.

noun:Angel.tx: From Middle High German angel, from Old High German angul, from Proto-Germanic *angulō, *angô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enk- (“something bent, hook”). Compare Dutch angel, hengel, English angle.

noun:Angst.tx: From Middle High German angest, from Old High German angust, from Proto-Germanic *angustiz.

noun:Anime.tx: Borrowed from Japanese アニメ (anime), an abbreviation of アニメーション (animēshon), ultimately from English animation.

noun:Anion.tx: Borrowed from English anion, indirectly from Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “upwards”) + ἰόν (ión, “wandering”) because anions wander towards the anode (the place of higher electrical potential).

noun:Anke.tx: From Middle High German anko, from Old High German ancha. Related to Enkel (“ankle”).

noun:Arm.tx: From Middle High German arm, from Old High German arm, from Proto-West Germanic *arm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ermos, *h₂ŕ̥mos, an extension of *h₂er- (“to fit together, to link, to join”). Cognate with Dutch arm, English arm, Swedish arm, Yiddish אָרעם (orem). The Indo-European root is also the source of Latin armus and arma.

noun:Art.tx: From Middle High German art, from Old High German *art, from Proto-West Germanic *ard, from Proto-Germanic *ardiz.

noun:Artist.tx: Early 14th century, borrowed from Medieval Latin artista (“artist”). The modern meaning “circus player” developed in the 19th century under influence from French artiste.

noun:As.tx: Borrowed from Latin as. Doublet of below As.

noun:Aspirin.tx: From acetylierte Spirsäure (literally “acetylated salicylic acid”). The second word is from the plant name Spiraea.

noun:Aster.tx: Borrowed from Latin astēr (“star”). Doublet of Star and Stern.

noun:Atem.tx: From Middle High German ātem, from Old High German ātum, from Proto-West Germanic *ādm, *āþm, from Proto-Germanic *ēþmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eh₁tmén-. Cognate with Dutch adem and Old English ǣþm. Doublet of Odem. Final unstressed -em (except in the adjectival dative ending) regularly becomes -en in Late Middle High German; compare Boden, Faden. The corresponding form āten is attested, …

noun:Atlas.tx: Borrowed from Latin Atlās or from Ancient Greek Ἄτλας (Átlas), from the name of the mythological figure Ἄτλας (Átlas, “Bearer (of the Heavens)”).

noun:Atoll.tx: Borrowed from English atoll, from Portuguese atol, from Dhivehi އަތޮޅު (atoḷu).

noun:Atom.tx: Borrowed from Latin atomus, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos).

noun:Aubergine.tx: Unadapted borrowing from French aubergine. Doublet of Melanzani.

noun:Aura.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin aura, ultimately from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra).

noun:Aus.tx: Calque of English out. Doublet of Out.

noun:Auto.tx: Clipping of Automobil, from French automobile.

noun:Autobus.tx: From French autobus, analyzable as Auto + Bus.

noun:Autor.tx: From New Latin autor, from Latin auctor. See there for more. Compare English author, French auteur.

noun:Aversion.tx: Borrowed from French aversion, from Latin āversiō.

noun:Avocado.tx: From older (still regional) Spanish avocado, folk-etymologically altered byform of aguacate, which see.

noun:Axiom.tx: From Latin axiōma, Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα (axíōma)

noun:Aas.tx: From Middle High German ās (“carrion, bait”), from Old High German *ās, from Proto-Germanic *ēsą. Later merged with Middle High German āȥ (“food”), from Old High German āȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *āt, from Proto-Germanic *ētą. Both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- (“to eat”).

noun:Arsch.tx: From Middle High German ars, from Old High German ars, from Proto-West Germanic *ars. Cognate with Dutch aars, English arse. The alternative neuter gender in the figurative sense probably from a backformation from Arschloch (“arsehole”).

noun:Arschloch.tx: From Middle High German arsloch, from Old High German arsloh. Equivalent to Arsch (“arse, ass”) + Loch (“hole”).

verb:abstoßen.tx: From Middle High German abestōzen, from Old High German abastōzan. Equivalent to ab- + stoßen.

adj:ägyptisch.tx: From Middle High German ēgiptisch, from Old High German egyptisk. By surface analysis, Ägypten + -isch.

adj:ähnlich.tx: From Middle High German anelich, enlich (“alike”), from Old High German *analīh (attested in derivatives), a contraction of anagilīh, from Proto-Germanic *anagalīkaz, from *ana (“on”) + *galīkaz (“like”), that is “almost identical”. Compare German angleichen. Cognate with Middle Dutch aenlijck, English alike, Old Norse álíkr. The contemporary form is possibly from a merger of Middle High German …

verb:abschreiben.tx: From Middle High German abeschrīben. Equivalent to ab- + schreiben.

verb:ärgern.tx: Inherited from Middle High German argern (“worsen”), from Old High German argerōn, derived from arg (“bad”). Compare English eerie.

noun:Angsthase.tx: From Angst (“fear”) + Hase (“hare”). The compound could simply be based on the hare’s flight instinct, but is usually thought to be an alteration of unattested *Angsthose, from Hose (“trousers, pants”); compare German Bangbüxe, Dutch bangebroek, English scaredy pants.

noun:Amtsschimmel.tx: Perhaps from Amt + Simile (from Latin simile (“similar”, neuter singular), from similis), the name of a standardized form used by the bureaucracy of the Austrian Empire. Alternatively, perhaps a reference to the service horses (Amt (“official”) + -s- + Schimmel (“white horse”)) which were provided in Switzerland and elsewhere to government officials.

verb:ablassen.tx: From Middle High German abelāzen, abelān, from Old High German oblāzan. Equivalent to ab- + lassen.

noun:Abenteuer.tx: From Middle High German âventiure, borrowed from Old French aventure and like the latter originally feminine. The neuter gender is from Middle Low German.

verb:abfahren.tx: From Middle High German abevarn, from Old High German abafaran, from Proto-West Germanic *abafaran. Equivalent to ab- (“from”) + fahren (“drive”). Cognate with Dutch afvaren.

noun:Abfahrt.tx: Verbal noun of abfahren (“to depart, to drive down”). By surface analysis, ab- + Fahrt.

verb:auslassen.tx: From Middle High German ūzlāzen, from Old High German ūzlāzan. Equivalent to aus- (“out”) + lassen (“to let”).

verb:anfangen.tx: From Middle High German anevāhen, from Old High German anafāhan, from Proto-West Germanic *anafą̄han. Equivalent to an- + fangen.

verb:antworten.tx: From Middle High German antwürten, from Old High German antwurten, from Proto-Germanic *andawurdijaną. By surface analysis, Antwort + -en.

verb:aufmachen.tx: From Middle High German ūfmachen. Equivalent to auf- + machen.

noun:Aar.tx: From Middle High German ar, arn, from Old High German aro, arn, from Proto-West Germanic *arō, from Proto-Germanic *arô.

noun:Amme.tx: From Middle High German amme, from Old High German amma, from Proto-West Germanic *ammā, from Proto-Germanic *ammǭ (“mother”).

adv:auch.tx: From Middle High German ouch, from Old High German ouh, from Proto-Germanic *auk. Cognate with Dutch ook (“also”), Low German ook (“also”), West Frisian ek (“also, too”), Luxembourgish och (“also”), Swedish och (“and”), Icelandic og (“and”), Danish og (“and”), and archaic English eke (“also”).

intj:auch.tx: From Middle High German ouch, from Old High German ouh, from Proto-Germanic *auk. Cognate with Dutch ook (“also”), Low German ook (“also”), West Frisian ek (“also, too”), Luxembourgish och (“also”), Swedish och (“and”), Icelandic og (“and”), Danish og (“and”), and archaic English eke (“also”).

noun:Abnahme.tx: Back-formation from abnehmen on the basis of Nahme.

noun:Abfall.tx: From Middle High German abfal, abefal, equivalent to ab- (“from”) + Fall (“fall”). Cognate with German Low German Offall, Dutch afval, English offal, Swedish avfall. Compare typologically Bulgarian отпадък (otpadăk), Czech otpad, Serbo-Croatian отпад (< Proto-Slavic *otъpadъ < *otъ + *padati). Also compare French déchet (<< Latin dēcidō < dē- + cadō).

noun:Anatomie.tx: Borrowed from Latin anatomia, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομία (anatomía), from ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “dissection”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, incise”).

noun:Abdecker.tx: Originally “the person that strips the hide (back then called Decke) from a perished animal”.

verb:abdecken.tx: From Middle High German abedecken. Equivalent to ab- + decken. Cognate with Dutch afdekken (“to cover”).

noun:Ampel.tx: From Middle High German ampel, ampolle, ampulle, from Old High German ampla, ampulla (“vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *ampullā (“flask, cruse”). The sense development was vessel → hanging lamp (in or shaped like a vessel) → traffic light. Doublet of Ampulle.

noun:Ameise.tx: *From Middle High German āmeiȥe, from Old High German āmeiȥa, from Proto-West Germanic *āmaitijā. Cognate with English ant, Scots emmot (“ant”), dialectal Dutch emt, empt (“ant”). *(electric pallet jack): From the trademark "Ameise", a brand of the Jungheinrich German company for electric pallet jacks.

num:achtzehn.tx: From Middle High German ahzehen, from Old High German ahtozehan, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutehun. Equivalent to acht + zehn. Compare Dutch achttien, West Frisian achttjin, English eighteen, Danish atten.

num:achtzig.tx: From Middle High German ahzec, from Old High German ahtozug, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutēhundą. Equivalent to acht + -zig.

noun:Anhang.tx: From Middle High German anehanc. By surface analysis, an- + Hang.

noun:Abendstern.tx: From Middle High German ābentsterne, from Old High German ābandsterno, from Proto-West Germanic *ābanþsternō, from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþsternǭ. Equivalent to Abend (“evening”) + Stern (“star”).

noun:Albtraum.tx: Alb + Traum, because nightmares in some forms of German folklore are thought to be caused by an elf sitting on one's chest while one slept.

verb:angeln.tx: See Angel. Compare Dutch hengelen, English angle.

noun:Achat.tx: From Middle High German achāt. Cognate with Latin achātēs.

noun:Anschauung.tx: From Middle High German anschouwunge, calque of Latin vīsiō; analysable as anschauen + -ung.

noun:Ähre.tx: From Middle High German eher, äher n, from Old High German ehir, ahir, ahar n, from Proto-Germanic *ahaz n. The form with Ä- is Upper German, where -h- led to an open vowel through secondary (rather than primary) umlaut. The feminine form, in turn, is a chiefly Central German backformation from plural use. Cognate with Dutch aar, West Frisian ier, English ear. Ultimately derived from …

noun:Amelie.tx: Derived from Proto-Germanic compound names beginning with the element *amal (“vigor”).

verb:abbiegen.tx: From Middle High German abebiegen. Equivalent to ab- + biegen.

verb:abbilden.tx: From Middle High German abebilden, abebileden. Equivalent to ab- + bilden. Compare Dutch afbeelden.

verb:abbinden.tx: From Middle High German abebinden. Equivalent to ab- + binden.

noun:Arbeit.tx: From Middle High German arbeit, from Old High German arbeit, from Proto-West Germanic *arbaiþi, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidiz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan, servant, slave”), from which English orphan is also derived. Cognate with Yiddish אַרבעט (arbet), Middle English arveth.

noun:Auster.tx: Attested a few times in Old High German, but only much later effectively introduced via Middle Low German ūster, from Middle Dutch oester. The Dutch word is borrowed from Latin ostrea, itself from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon) (pertaining to ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”), ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “shell”)). Compare Old English ostre, Old French oistre (modern French huître).

pron:alles.tx: From Middle High German alles, allez, from Old High German allez, allaz, neuter form of al, all (“all”), equivalent to all + -es. Compare Low German allns (Allns), Dutch alles, West Frisian alles, Gothic 𐌰𐌻𐌻𐌰𐍄𐌰 (allata).

adj:allein.tx: From Middle High German al-ein. Cognate with Middle English al-one, English alone, Dutch alleen, Low German alleene (Münsterländisch), alläine (Sauerländisch).

adv:allein.tx: From Middle High German al-ein. Cognate with Middle English al-one, English alone, Dutch alleen, Low German alleene (Münsterländisch), alläine (Sauerländisch).

conj:allein.tx: From Middle High German al-ein. Cognate with Middle English al-one, English alone, Dutch alleen, Low German alleene (Münsterländisch), alläine (Sauerländisch).

verb:achten.tx: From Middle High German ahten, from Old High German ahtōn, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtōn, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtu. Equivalent to Acht (“attention”) + -en.

noun:Arbeitsfläche.tx: From Arbeit, the interfix -s, and Fläche.

adj:arg.tx: From Middle High German arc, from Old High German arg. Compare Hunsrik aarich, Pennsylvania German arrig, Central Franconian ärch, and Dutch erg. Also etymologically linked is English eerie.

verb:ausweisen.tx: From Middle High German ūzweizen, from Old High German ūzwīsen. By surface analysis, aus- + weisen.

verb:ändern.tx: From Middle High German endern, more at anderer (“other, different”). Cognate with Hunsrik ennre.

noun:Abwasser.tx: From Middle High German abewaȥȥer, equivalent to ab- + Wasser.

noun:Abstand.tx: ab- + Stand. Cognate with English offstand (“offset, restitution”).

noun:Absicht.tx: Attested since the 17th century, nominalization of absehen

prep:außer.tx: From Middle High German ūȥer, from Old High German ūȥar. More at aus. Cf. English outer, Norwegian uten-, ytre.

conj:außer.tx: From Middle High German ūȥer, from Old High German ūȥar. More at aus. Cf. English outer, Norwegian uten-, ytre.

noun:Ader.tx: From Middle High German āder, from Old High German ādra, from Proto-West Germanic *ādrā. Akin to Saterland Frisian Äddere, Danish åre, Dutch ader, English edder, Middle English edre and Icelandic æð (from Old Norse æðr).

noun:Asphalt.tx: Borrowed from French asphalte, from Late Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”).

prep:außerhalb.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ūȥerhalp, from Old High German ūȥarhalb. By surface analysis, außer- + halb.

adv:außerhalb.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ūȥerhalp, from Old High German ūȥarhalb. By surface analysis, außer- + halb.

conj:anstatt.tx: From an (“on”) + Statt (“stead”). Compare English instead.

prep:anstatt.tx: From an (“on”) + Statt (“stead”). Compare English instead.

noun:Ahorn.tx: From Middle High German ahorn, from Old High German ahorn, possibly from Proto-West Germanic *ahurn. Perhaps cognate with Latin acer.

verb:atmen.tx: From Middle High German ātemen, from Old High German ātamōn, derived from Proto-Germanic *ēþmaz. By surface analysis, Atem + -en. Cognate with Dutch ademen.

adv:außen.tx: From Middle High German ūȥen, from Old High German ūȥana. Compare archaic English outen.

verb:anziehen.tx: Compound of an- (“on, at”) + ziehen (“pull”). To the western German idiom sich etwas anziehen von compare Dutch zich iets aantrekken van.

noun:Acker.tx: From Middle High German acker, from Old High German ackar (“field”), from Proto-West Germanic *akr.

noun:Achse.tx: From Middle High German ahse, from Old High German ahsa, from Proto-West Germanic *ahsu.

noun:Axt.tx: From Middle High German ackes, from Old High German ackus, itself from Proto-West Germanic *akusi, while ultimately descending from Proto-Germanic *akwisī. Compare Low German Ax, Dutch aks, English axe, Danish økse, Swedish yxa, Icelandic öxi.

verb:auflösen.tx: From auf- + lösen. Compare Dutch oplossen.

noun:Ablass.tx: From ab + Lass, from lassen (“to allow”).

adj:äußere.tx: From Middle High German ūʒer, from Old High German ūzaro.

noun:Abtei.tx: From Middle High German aptīe, abbeteie, from Old High German abbateia (manuscript 12th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *abbadejā (“abbey”). Analysable as Abt + -ei. The early ei-spellings are unusual, but perhaps caused by the hiatus; regular ī-forms are found alongside in Middle High German.

noun:Achsel.tx: From Old High German ahsala, ahsla, from Proto-Germanic *ahslō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis”). Cognate with Old Norse ǫxl (“shoulder”) and ǫxull (“axle”) (whence Danish aksel, Icelandic öxl), English axle. Also cognate with Latin āxilla (“shoulder joint”), Sanskrit अक्ष (ákṣa, “axle”).

noun:Ahle.tx: From Middle High German āle, Old High German āla, from Proto-West Germanic *ālu, from Proto-Germanic *ēlō.

noun:Ahn.tx: From Middle High German an, ane, from Old High German ano, from Proto-Germanic *anô (“forefather”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en- (“ancestor”). Cognate with Latin anus.

noun:Almosen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German almuosen, from Old High German alamuosa, from Proto-West Germanic *alemōsinā, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *alēmosyna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “pitiful, merciful”) + -σῠ́νη (-sŭ́nē). The modern vocalism is from Middle Low German almōse.

noun:Amboss.tx: From Middle High German anebōȥ, from Old High German anabōȥ (“anvil”) (see also anabolz (“anvil”), anabelzi (“anvil”), which are cognate to Plautdietsch Aumbolt (“anvil”)). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bautaną.

noun:Alm.tx: The form suggests a Bavarian influence (cf. German Taube vs Bavarian Daum (“dove”)). From Middle High German alben, the oblique form of albe, from Old High German alba. Doublet of Alp. Compare Bavarian Alm, Alemannic German Alp, Alpe.

noun:Amt.tx: From Middle High German ambahte, ambehte, ambet, ammet, ampt, ambt, amt, from Old High German ambahti, ambaht, from Proto-West Germanic *ambaht, from Proto-Germanic *ambahtaz, from Gaulish ambaxtos, from Proto-Celtic *ambaxtos. The Middle High German contracted form amb(e)t developed quite regularly, via also attested ammet or ambt, into modern German Amt. Cognate with Dutch ambacht and ambt, …

noun:Amsel.tx: From Middle High German amsel, from Old High German amsala, from Proto-West Germanic *amslā.

noun:Anker.tx: From Middle High German anker, from Old High German anker, ankero, from Proto-West Germanic *ankurō, from Proto-Germanic *ankurô.

noun:Antwort.tx: From Middle High German antwürte, from Old High German antwurti, from Proto-Germanic *andawurdiją. The gender change from neuter to feminine is due to semantic association with Frage (“question”). See also antworten. Cognate to Dutch antwoord and Afrikaans antwoord.

noun:Apostel.tx: From Old High German apostolo, from Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos).

noun:Ast.tx: From Middle High German ast, from Old High German ast, from Proto-West Germanic *ast, from Proto-Germanic *astaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ósdos (“branch”).

noun:Ärmel.tx: From Old High German armilo (“armband”); equivalent to Arm (“arm”) + -el.

verb:ahnen.tx: From Middle High German anen, from Old High German *anōn, from Proto-West Germanic *anōn, from *ana (“on”, preposition), from Proto-Germanic *an (“on”). Cognate with Middle Low German ānen (whence German Low German ahnen (“to suspect, guess”)), dialectal Dutch anen (“to conjecture, tell, calculate”), Saterland Frisian oanje (“to suspect, guess”).

verb:anbieten.tx: From Middle High German anebieten. Equivalent to an- + bieten.

noun:Aufsatz.tx: From Middle High German ūfsaz; analyzable as a back-formation from aufsetzen. Cognate with Luxembourgish Opsaz, Dutch opstel.

noun:Amerikaner.tx: From Amerika + -er, with an additional n, or from Latin americānus + -er.

adj:aufmerksam.tx: From aufmerken (“to observe”) + -sam, the former component from auf- (“up-”) + merken (“to notice”).

noun:Akt.tx: Borrowed from Latin āctus. The artistic sense derives from the 19th century practice of sketching models carrying out actions, for which the models would usually be nude.

noun:Anfang.tx: From Middle High German anvanc, anevanc, from Old High German anafang, from Proto-West Germanic *anafangi. See German anfangen, Dutch aanvang, English fang.

noun:Augapfel.tx: From Middle High German ougapfel, from Old High German ougapful, augaphul, from Proto-West Germanic *augapl, equivalent to Auge (“eye”) + Apfel (“apple”). Cognate with Old English ēagæppel (“apple of the eye; pupil”).

noun:Auftritt.tx: From Middle High German ūftrit (“height”); related to treten (“to step; to kick”). Cognate with Luxembourgish Optrëtt and Norwegian Bokmål opptrinn.

noun:Achterbahn.tx: Achter (“an eight”) + Bahn (“route”), from the figure-eight shape commonly seen in roller coasters, particularly older ones.

verb:abschneiden.tx: From Middle High German abesnīden, from Old High German abasnīdan. Equivalent to ab- + schneiden. Cognate to Dutch afsnijden.

noun:Äther.tx: 16th century, from Latin aethēr, from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr).

adv:allerdings.tx: Compound of aller (genitive plural of alle (“all”)) + Dings (genitive singular of Ding (“thing”)) (compare schlechterdings). Before the 19th century, the full form aller Dinge (“of all things”), with the plural Dinge, was used.

noun:Ackermann.tx: From Middle High German ackerman, from Old High German ackarman, from Proto-Germanic *akramann-. Equivalent to Acker (“field”) + Mann (“man”). Cognate with English acreman.

noun:Astronomie.tx: Unadapted borrowing from French astronomie, from Latin astronomia.

adj:antik.tx: Borrowed from French antique, from Latin antīquus.

noun:Apotheke.tx: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē). Doublet of Bodega, Bottich, and Boutique.

verb:abkacken.tx: ab- (“off, away, out”) + kacken (“to crap, to shit”). Compare English crap out.

adj:allerlei.tx: From all (“all”) + -erlei. Cognate with Dutch allerlei.

noun:Albanese.tx: From Italian albanese (“Albanian”). Equivalent to Albanien + -ese.

noun:Aufruhr.tx: From Middle High German ūfruor, from Middle Low German uprōr. Compare Dutch oproer, English uproar.

noun:Arschgeweih.tx: From Arsch (“arse”) + Geweih (“antler, horns”). Cf. Dutch aarsgewei and English arse antlers.

noun:Alkohol.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin alcohol, ultimately from Arabic الكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”).

noun:Armbrust.tx: From Middle High German armbrust (12th century, variants armbrost, armborst, armbrast, armbst), from Medieval Latin arbalista, from Late Latin arcuballista, from Latin arcus (“bow”) + ballista (“ancient military engine for hurling missiles”) (compare English arbalest); modified, possibly by folk etymology, but as Grimm notes, the German noun was neuter well into the early modern period which …

noun:Angriff.tx: From Middle High German angrif, anegrif, from Old High German *anagrif, from Proto-West Germanic *anagripi, equivalent to an- + Griff. Related to German angreifen.

verb:abkommen.tx: From Middle High German abekomen, from Old High German abaqueman, from ab- (“from”) + kweman (“to come”). The sense "grow gaunt" is attested since the 15th century as a shortening of the phrase "vom Fleisch abkommen". The specifically Namibian use is a loan meaning from Afrikaans afkom.

noun:Anwalt.tx: From Middle High German anwalde, from Old High German anawalto, from Old English ānweald (“power, empire”).

noun:Anzug.tx: From Middle High German anzuc, verbal noun of aneziehen. Equivalent to an- + Zug.

noun:Assel.tx: From Middle High German esel, somehow related to ëȥȥen (“to eat”).

verb:anzünden.tx: Compound of an- (“on, at”) + zünden (“to ignite, kindle”). Akin to Old English ontendan, Swedish antända, Norwegian antenne.

noun:Aderlass.tx: From Middle High German āderlāʒ, āderlæʒe. Equivalent to Ader (“vein”) + the stem of lassen (“to let”).

noun:Automat.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin automatum, from Ancient Greek αὐτόμᾰτος (autómătos)

intj:ade.tx: From Middle High German adē, from Old French adieu. Doublet of tschö.

adj:aufrecht.tx: From Middle High German ūfreht, from Old High German ūfreht. Analyzable as auf + recht. Compare Dutch oprecht, English upright.

noun:Anfall.tx: Deverbal noun from anfallen (“to set upon, attack, overwhelm”).

noun:Auerhahn.tx: From Middle High German ū̆rhan, influenced by ūr (“aurochs”) (from Old High German ūro, from Proto-West Germanic *ūr) and originally orhan, ultimately from the root of Auerhuhn, which see.

noun:Aristokratie.tx: From Medieval Latin aristocratia, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατίᾱ (aristokratíā, “the rule of the best“, that is, “the best-born”, “nobility”), equivalent to Ancient Greek ἄριστος (áristos, “best”) + -kratie.

noun:Anarchismus.tx: Probably borrowed from French anarchisme. By surface analysis, Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “not”) + Ancient Greek ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”) + -ismus.

verb:aussehen.tx: From Middle High German ūzsehen. Analysable as aus- (“out”) + sehen (“to see”). Compare Yiddish אויסזען (oyszen), Dutch uitzien, Norwegian Nynorsk sjå ut, Swedish se ut, Danish se ud.

verb:ausreißen.tx: From Middle High German ūzrīzen, from Old High German ūzrīzan. Equivalent to aus- + reißen. (to run away): Compare typologically Russian удира́ть (udirátʹ), да́ть дёру (dátʹ djóru) (akin to драть (dratʹ)); also compare рвану́ть (rvanútʹ), сорва́ться (sorvátʹsja) (akin to рвать (rvatʹ)), ломану́ть (lomanútʹ), ломану́ться (lomanútʹsja) (akin to ломи́ть (lomítʹ)).

verb:ausrotten.tx: From aus- (“out”) + rotten (“to clear woods”), the latter was a more southern variant of roden, from Middle High German roten, roden, from Proto-Germanic *rudōną.

verb:ausmerzen.tx: Equivalent to aus (“out”) + an unknown element. There are several theories: * From Middle High German merzen (“to trade”), derived from Latin merx (“merchandise”); thus “to remove from commerce, from one’s assortment”. * From März (“March”), because in some regions animals unfit for breeding were singled out from the stock during this month. * From *merksen, from merken (“to mark, notice”) + …

adj:albern.tx: From Middle High German alwære, from Old High German alawāri (“friendly, good-natured”), from a compound of Proto-Germanic *allaz (“all”) + *wēraz (“true; friendly”). The final -n is an original case ending that was added to the stem in German Low German territory (compare schüchtern). Close cognate with Gothic 𐌰𐌻𐌻𐌰𐍅𐌴𐍂𐌴𐌹 (allawērei, “sincerity, simplicity”); for a similar semantic association …

noun:Alltag.tx: From Middle High German altac, alltag, alletag; also analysed as All (“all”) + Tag (“day”).

noun:Anreiz.tx: Deverbal from anreizen (“to arouse (in someone the desire to do something)”), itself from an- + reizen.

adj:allmächtig.tx: From Middle High German almehtec, from Old High German almahtīg, alamahtīg, from Proto-West Germanic *alamahtīg, from Proto-Germanic *alamahtīgaz. Equivalent to all (“all”) + -mächtig (“mighty”). Synchronically also analyzable as Allmacht (“omnipotence”) + -ig, although Allmacht in fact represents a back-formation from the adjective. Cognates include Dutch almachtig, English almighty, and Old …

noun:Aktie.tx: Borrowed from Dutch actie (“stock”), from Middle Dutch actie (“legal claim”), from Latin āctiō. Doublet of Aktion and Action. An earlier borrowing in the sense “legal claim” remained restricted to north-western Germany. In Dutch itself, both of the mentioned senses are obsolete.

noun:Augenblick.tx: From Middle High German ougenblic (12th c. as “glance, look”, ca. 1300 in temporal use). By surface analysis, Auge (“eye”) + -n- + Blick (“glance”). Compare Yiddish אויגנבליק (oygnblik), Luxembourgish Abléck, Dutch ogenblik, Middle Low German ôgenblick (whence Danish øjeblik etc.). Semantically cf. also English blink of an eye.

intj:Augenblick.tx: From Middle High German ougenblic (12th c. as “glance, look”, ca. 1300 in temporal use). By surface analysis, Auge (“eye”) + -n- + Blick (“glance”). Compare Yiddish אויגנבליק (oygnblik), Luxembourgish Abléck, Dutch ogenblik, Middle Low German ôgenblick (whence Danish øjeblik etc.). Semantically cf. also English blink of an eye.

noun:Ausnahme.tx: Deverbal from ausnehmen (“to exempt, to except”).

noun:Akku.tx: Clipping of Akkumulator. Compare Finnish akku.

noun:Attentat.tx: Borrowed and relatinized from French attentat, from Latin attentātum, attemptātum (“attempt; attempted crime”), derived from attentō, attemptō. May have been reinterpreted as a complex noun, with the second component being Tat (“deed, act, crime”).

noun:Ausdruck.tx: Backformation from ausdrücken (“to express”), itself a calque of Latin exprimō. Analysable as aus- (“out”) + Druck (“pressing, pressure”).

noun:Automatikgetriebe.tx: Calque of English automatic transmission, from Automatik + Getriebe.

noun:Archiv.tx: From Late Latin archīvum (“public records office”).

verb:ankommen.tx: From Middle High German anekomen, from Old High German anaqueman, from Proto-West Germanic *anakweman, from Proto-Germanic *anakwemaną (“to come to, come at, arrive”). Compare Dutch aankomen, English oncome, Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐌰𐌵𐌹𐌼𐌰𐌽 (anaqiman).

noun:Ausschuss.tx: From Middle High German ūȥschuȥ, synchronically analyzed as a deverbal from ausschießen (“to stand out”); see aus- (“out-”) + schießen (“to shoot”) for more. Compare typologically Latin ēiectāmenta (< ēiectō), Russian отбро́сы (otbrósy) (< отбро́сить (otbrósitʹ)).

noun:Anruf.tx: From Middle High German aneruof, from Old High German anaruof, anahruof. By surface analysis, deverbal from anrufen (literally “calling, ringing”).

noun:Angebot.tx: 18th-century alteration of Anbot, from Middle High German anbot, anpot (14th c.). Compare Dutch aanbod, Middle Low German anbot. Deverbal from anbieten (“to offer”). The alteration is due to the general replacement of the noun Bot (from Old High German bot and Proto-Germanic *budą) with prefixed Gebot; hence by surface analysis, an- + Gebot.

noun:Auszeit.tx: From aus- (“out”) + Zeit (“time”). Cognate with Alemannic German Uusziit.

noun:Architekt.tx: Borrowed from Latin architectus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn).

noun:Astrologie.tx: Borrowed from Latin astrologia, equivalent to astro- + -logie.

noun:Allerheiligen.tx: Univerbation of aller Heiligen (“All Saints', of all saints”), calque of Latin omnium sānctōrum, in festum omnium sānctōrum (“feast of all saints”).

noun:Aufstand.tx: Equivalent to auf- (“upwards”) + Stand (“standing, position”); compare aufstehen (“to rebel, rise up”).

noun:Aussicht.tx: From aus- (“out”) + Sicht (“sight”). Compare Dutch uitzicht.

noun:Anarchie.tx: Via French anarchie and Medieval Latin anarchia, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía), from ἀν- (an-, “not”), + ἀρχός (arkhós, “ruler, authority”).

noun:Aktivist.tx: From English activist. By surface analysis, aktiv + -ist. The East German title is short for Aktivist der sozialistischen Arbeit (literally “activist of socialist work”).

noun:Allheilmittel.tx: Equivalent to all (“all”) + heilen (“heal”) + Mittel (“means, substance”).

noun:Annullierung.tx: From annullieren (“to annul, nullify, cancel”) + -ung (“-ing”) (compare Yiddish אַנולירונג (anulirung)).

verb:annullieren.tx: Ultimately from Latin annullō (“to annihilate, annul”) (compare Yiddish אַנולירן (anulirn)), from ad (“to”) + nūllus (“none, not any”).

verb:angreifen.tx: From Middle High German anegrīfen (“to grab, seize upon, violate, assault, attack”), from Old High German anagrīfan (“to touch, grab, seize, attack”), from Proto-West Germanic *anagrīpan (“to seize, attack”), equivalent to an- + greifen. Cognate with German Low German angriepen, Dutch aangrijpen, Old English ongripe (“an attack, assault”).

noun:Antithese.tx: From Latin antithesis. By surface analysis, anti (“anti-”) + These (“thesis”)

adj:angemessen.tx: Past participle of anmessen (“to make fit”), from an- + messen.

adv:angemessen.tx: Past participle of anmessen (“to make fit”), from an- + messen.

noun:Amnestie.tx: Borrowed from Latin amnēstia, from Ancient Greek ἀμνηστία (amnēstía).

noun:Augenbraue.tx: From Middle High German ougebrā (ougenbrā, ougenbrāwe), from ouge + brā; equivalent to Auge (“eye”) + -n- + Braue (“brow”).

verb:anbeten.tx: From Middle High German anebeten, from Old High German anabetōn. Equivalent to an- (“on”) + beten (“pray”). Cognate with Dutch aanbidden. For structural similarity compare Latin adoro.

verb:aufspringen.tx: From Middle High German ūfspringen. Equivalent to auf- + springen.

noun:Alchemie.tx: Borrowed from Latin alchēmia, from Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ).

noun:Archäologie.tx: From Latin archaeologia, from Ancient Greek ἀρχαιολογίᾱ (arkhaiologíā).

noun:Authentizität.tx: From authentisch (“authentic”) + -ität (“-ity”). Ultimately from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós)

adj:archaisch.tx: From Late Latin archaicus, itself from Ancient Greek ἀρχαϊκός (arkhaïkós).

noun:Abgrund.tx: From Middle High German abgrunt, Old High German abgrunti. Cognate with Gothic 𐌰𐍆𐌲𐍂𐌿𐌽𐌳𐌹𐌸𐌰 (afgrundiþa).

verb:auflegen.tx: From Middle High German ūflegen, from Old High German ūfleggen, from Proto-West Germanic *upplaggjan. Equivalent to auf- + legen.

noun:Aussteuer.tx: Deverbal from aussteuern, from Middle High German ūzstiuren (“to equip, furnish”). Analysable as aus- + Steuer.

verb:anleiten.tx: From Middle High German anleiten, aneleiten, from Old High German analeiten, from Proto-West Germanic *analaidijan, from Proto-Germanic *analaidijaną. Equivalent to an- + leiten. Cognates include Dutch aanleiden and English onlead.

noun:Atmosphäre.tx: From New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “steam”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”).

noun:Armee.tx: Early 16th century, borrowed from Middle French armee. Compare Modern French armée, English army.

noun:Auszug.tx: From Middle High German ūȥzuc. Equivalent to a deverbal from ausziehen.

noun:Absolutismus.tx: Borrowed from French absolutisme. By surface analysis, absolut + -ismus.

noun:Autismus.tx: Coined by Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler in 1911, from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós, “self”) + -ισμός (-ismós, “-ism”).

adj:aberwitzig.tx: From Aberwitz + -ig, from Middle High German aberwitze, from aber (“opposite, contrary”) + witze (“knowledge, sense”).

adv:aberwitzig.tx: From Aberwitz + -ig, from Middle High German aberwitze, from aber (“opposite, contrary”) + witze (“knowledge, sense”).

verb:abheben.tx: From Middle High German abheben, abeheben, equivalent to ab- (“off-”) + heben (“to lift, raise”). Cognate with Old Saxon afhebbian (whence Middle Low German afhebben).

noun:Apparat.tx: 15th century, from Latin apparātus, perhaps in part through somewhat earlier Middle Low German appārāt (14th c.). See English apparatus for more.

noun:Aktivität.tx: From French activité (“activity”), from Medieval Latin āctīvitās (“activity, movement”), from Latin āctīvus (“active”). Compare aktiv (“active”) + -ität.

noun:Aberglaube.tx: From Middle High German abergloube, from aber (“behind”) and gloube (“belief”).

adj:abergläubisch.tx: From Middle High German *abergloubisch, equivalent to Aberglaube + -isch. Cognate with Middle Low German āverlȫvisch (“superstitious”).

noun:Arier.tx: Borrowed from Sanskrit आर्य (ārya, “noble”). More at Aryan.

adj:autoritär.tx: From Autorität or from French autoritaire.

noun:Adidas.tx: Named after the company founder Adolf „Adi“ Dassler.

verb:absetzen.tx: From Middle High German abesetzen. Equivalent to ab- + setzen.

noun:Apoplexie.tx: From Late Latin poplexia, apoplexia, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξίᾱ (apoplēxíā), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō, “to cripple by a stroke”); ἀπο- (apo-, “from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”).

noun:Apostroph.tx: From earlier Apostrophus m, from Latin apostrophus f.

verb:applaudieren.tx: 16th century, from Latin applaudere, in part through Middle French applaudir.

noun:Akteur.tx: Borrowed from French acteur, from Latin āctor, from agere, whence German agieren.

adj:arktisch.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin arcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀρκτικός (arktikós).

verb:aufschlagen.tx: From Middle High German ūfslahen, from Old High German ūfslahan. Equivalent to auf- + schlagen.

noun:Ambivalenz.tx: Coined by Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler in 1910, from Latin ambō (“both”) and valentia (“strength”), from the verb valeō (“to be strong”).

noun:Apfelsine.tx: Via Low German Appelsina, from Dutch appelsina (cp. appelsien, for which now usually sinaasappel). So named because of their introduction to Europe from China (Latin Sīna).

verb:abbrechen.tx: From Middle High German abebrëchen, from Old High German ababrëhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *ababrekan. Equivalent to ab- + brechen. Cognate with Dutch afbreken (“to demolish, to decompose”).

noun:Arznei.tx: From Middle High German arzenie. By surface analysis, Arzt + -ei. Compare Dutch artsenij.

noun:Akronym.tx: From akro- (“tip, end, beginning”) + -onym (“name”). First attested in the early 1900s. The term was modelled after Homonym and Synonym, and the parts are ultimately derived from Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “end, extremity”) and ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”).

noun:Anlage.tx: From anlegen (“to attach, apply, build, create, ...”).

verb:altern.tx: From Middle High German altern, from Old High German *altarōn (only attested as the past participle gialdaroda), from Proto-West Germanic *aldarōn.

verb:auswählen.tx: aus- (“out”) + wählen (“pick, choose, select”). Compare English pick out.

noun:Ausländer.tx: From Middle High German ūzlender, derived from ūzlant (“outlying fields”), by surface analysis, Ausland + -er. See aus, Länder. Modern German Ausland (“foreign countries”) is a back-formation from Ausländer. Compare archaic Dutch uitlander, English outlandish, outlander, Danish udlænding.

noun:Autopsie.tx: 18th century, from Ancient Greek αὐτοψία (autopsía). The specific contemporary sense (late 19th century) after French autopsie.

noun:Anstand.tx: From Middle High German anstand (“ceasefire; delay”), from an(e)stān. By surface analysis, deverbal from anstehen.

verb:anrufen.tx: From an- + rufen (“to call, to shout”).

adv:abends.tx: From Middle High German ābendes, adverbial genitive of ābent, whence modern German Abend (“evening”). From Abend + -s.

verb:abgeben.tx: From Middle High German *abegëben, from Old High German abagëban, from Proto-West Germanic *abageban, from Proto-Germanic *abagebaną; equivalent to ab- (“from”) + geben (“give”).

noun:Aktion.tx: 16th century, learned borrowing from Latin āctiō. Doublet of Action and Aktie.

noun:Absatz.tx: From Middle High German abesaz, analyzable as ab- + Satz.

verb:aufhören.tx: From Middle High German ūfhœren (“to stop”), equivalent to auf- (“up”) + hören (“to hear, listen, obey”). The sense is explained as a generalisation from “to obey a prohibition and desist”. Cognate with archaic Dutch ophoren, Yiddish אויפֿהערן (oyfhern), and Bavarian aufhearn. Compare also aufhorchen, preserving a more literal meaning.

verb:ausbrechen.tx: From Middle High German ūȥbrëchen, from Old High German ūȥbrëhhan. Equivalent to aus- + brechen.

noun:Anschlag.tx: Inherited from Middle High German anslac, from Old High German anaslag. By surface analysis, an- + Schlag.

noun:Analogie.tx: Borrowed from Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογία (analogía).

verb:ausschalten.tx: From Middle High German ūȥschalten, equivalent to aus- + schalten.

noun:Augenweide.tx: From Middle High German ougenweide. Equivalent to Auge (“eye”) + Weide (“meal”), the latter element being obsolete in this sense in modern German.

noun:Arachnophobie.tx: Borrowed from French arachnophobie, from Ancient Greek ἀράχνη (arákhnē, “spider”) + -phobie.

verb:aussprechen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ūȥsprëchen, Old High German ūȥsprëhhan, equivalent to aus- + sprechen.

adj:ausländisch.tx: From Middle High German ūzlendisch. Equivalent to Ausland + -isch; compare English outlandish.

noun:Amphibie.tx: From Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιον (amphíbion), from ἀμφί (amphí, “of both kinds”) + βίος (bíos, “life”). Can be found as a loanword in many European languages.

noun:Altweibersommer.tx: At least in the meaning "Indian summer", seemingly from alt (“old”) + Weiber (“women's”) + Sommer (“summer”), literally "old women's summer". Compare Hungarian vénasszonyok nyara, Polish babie lato, archaic Czech babské léto, Russian ба́бье ле́то (bábʹje léto), Belarusian ба́біна ле́та (bábina ljéta), Ukrainian ба́бине лі́то (bábyne líto), and English old wives' summer; compare also German …

noun:Äon.tx: 18th century, from Latin aeōn (“age, eternity”), from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, eternity”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu- (“vital force, life, long life, eternity”).

noun:Algorithmus.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin algorismus, influenced by Ancient Greek ἀριθμός (arithmós).

verb:angeben.tx: From Middle High German anegëben. Equivalent to an- + geben. Victor Klemperer notes in his Lingua Tertii Imperii that the sense of brag, boast is originally Yiddish.

noun:Attentäter.tx: From Attentat (“attack, assassination”) + -er, influenced by Täter (“doer, perpetrator”).

noun:Antibiotikum.tx: anti- or ἀντι- (anti-) + βιωτικός (biōtikós) (from βίος (bíos, “life”) + -τικός (-tikós)) + -us (in its neuter form)

noun:Allergie.tx: Coined by Austrian physician Clemens von Pirquet in 1906, from Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + Ancient Greek ἔργον (érgon, “work, activity”), on the model of Energie.

noun:Abonnent.tx: abonnieren + -ent without a French counterpart, since the second half of the 18th century.

noun:Anekdote.tx: From Ancient Greek ἀνέκδοτος (anékdotos), from ἀν- (an-, “not, un-”) + ἔκδοτος (ékdotos, “published”), from ἐκδίδωμι (ekdídōmi, “I publish”), from ἐκ- (ek-, “out”) + δίδωμι (dídōmi, “I give”).

noun:Akkordeon.tx: Coined and patented in May 1829 by Cyrill Demian as Accordion = Accord + -ion. The word then first became Akkordion in the 20th century, then Akkordeon under influence from French accordéon which in turn was influenced to be more similar to orphéon.

noun:Appetit.tx: Borrowed from Old French apetit or directly from its source, Late Latin appetītus (“attack; striving, desire; appetite”), a fourth-declension noun derived from Latin appetō (“to assail; to strive after”).

adj:aromatisch.tx: From Latin arōmaticus, from Ancient Greek ἀρωματικός (arōmatikós). By surface analysis, Aroma + -isch.

noun:Anagramm.tx: From Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “up, back”) + γράμμα (grámma, “letter”), equivalent to ana- + -gramm. Compare English anagram.

verb:ausgraben.tx: From Middle High German ūȥgraben, from Old High German ūȥgraban. Equivalent to aus- (“up”) + graben (“dig”). Cognate with Dutch uitgraven.

noun:Animosität.tx: From Latin animositas (“courage, spirit, vehemence”), equivalent to animos + -ität.

noun:Automobil.tx: Borrowed from French automobile. By surface analysis, auto- + mobil

adj:abwesend.tx: From Middle High German abwesende, abewesende, from Old High German abawesanti, present participle of Old High German abawesan (a calque of Latin abesse), but is chiefly restricted to Low German. Compare for this Dutch wezen (“to be”). The adjective stems from Middle Low German afwēsende and spreads southward during the 16th century.

verb:austreten.tx: From Middle High German ūztreten. Equivalent to aus- + treten.

verb:aushalten.tx: From Middle High German ūȥhalten. Equivalent to aus- + halten.

noun:Ausschank.tx: From ausschenken. Cognate with German Low German Utschank.

verb:aufgeben.tx: From Middle High German ūfgëben. Equivalent to auf- (“up”) + geben (“give”). Cognate with English upgive, Dutch opgeven.

noun:Aufgabe.tx: From Middle High German ūfgābe, verbal noun of ūfgëben, whence modern aufgeben. By surface analysis, auf (“up”) + Gabe (“gift, giving”).

noun:Abschnitt.tx: From Middle High German abesnit, from Old High German abesnit. By surface analysis, deverbal from abschneiden, equivalent to ab- + Schnitt.

verb:ackern.tx: From Middle High German ackern, ackeren, eckern, equivalent to Acker + -n. Cognate with Middle Low German ackeren, whence Low German ackern.

verb:auftreten.tx: From Middle High German ūftrëten. Equivalent to auf- + treten.

adv:außerdem.tx: Univerbation of außer + dem. Compare Latin praeterea.

adv:ansonsten.tx: Reinforcement of sonst by adding an- to the regional (Southern) sonsten. Since 18th.

conj:ansonsten.tx: Reinforcement of sonst by adding an- to the regional (Southern) sonsten. Since 18th.

adv:andernfalls.tx: Univerbation of anderen (“other”) + Falls (“case”), chiefly with syncope of the -e-. Originally an adverbial genitive.

conj:andernfalls.tx: Univerbation of anderen (“other”) + Falls (“case”), chiefly with syncope of the -e-. Originally an adverbial genitive.

noun:Aufbau.tx: Deverbal from aufbauen. Compare Dutch opbouw.

noun:Arzneimittel.tx: From Arznei + Mittel, since the end of the 16th century.

adj:angenehm.tx: an + genehm, from Old High German nami, ultimately from the same root as nehmen. Compare Sanskrit नमस्ते (namaste, “salutations (to you)”) for similar semantic development from the same Proto-Indo-European root.

verb:abhauen.tx: From Middle High German abehouwen, from Old High German abahouwan. Equivalent to ab- + hauen.

verb:auskommen.tx: aus- + kommen. For the western German sense compare Dutch uitkomen.

noun:Ausbau.tx: Back-formation from ausbauen. Also analyzable as aus- (“out”) + Bau (“construction”). Compare also Dutch uitbouw.

verb:äußern.tx: From Middle High German ūȥern, ūȥeren, that is, "making out (one's thoughts, etc.)"; see the related aus (“out”) for more.

noun:Alpaka.tx: Borrowed from Spanish alpaca, from Aymara allpaqa. Neuter gender probably after words like Kamel (“camel”), Pferd (“horse”), Schaf (“sheep”); compare the same development in Lama (now n, formerly also f).

adj:asiatisch.tx: Asiate/Asiat (“Asian person”) + -isch, or āsiāticus with -isch for -icus

noun:Abstinenz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German abstinencia, from Latin abstinentia.

noun:Abschluss.tx: From the verb abschließen. Analyzable as ab- + Schluss.

verb:anmachen.tx: From Middle High German anemachen. Equivalent to an- + machen.

noun:Artischocke.tx: From Northern Italian articiocco, from Provençal archichaut, arquichaut, from Old Spanish alcarchofa, from Andalusian Arabic خرشوف (ḵaršūf), from Arabic الْخُرْشُوف (al-ḵuršūf), definite form of خُرْشُوف (ḵuršūf).

noun:Akte.tx: Borrowed from Latin ācta (“negotiations, transactions”), from Latin agō (“to act, do, make”).

noun:Ansicht.tx: From ansehen but can be implicitly constructed as an- + Sicht.

noun:Anis.tx: From Middle High German anīs (“anise”), from Latin anīsum.

verb:ausscheiden.tx: From Middle High German ūzscheiden, from Old High German ūzskeiden, from Proto-West Germanic *ūtskaiþan, equivalent to aus- + scheiden. Cognate with German Low German utscheden.

noun:Ansporn.tx: Back-formation from anspornen, itself derived from Sporn (“spur”).

noun:Astronom.tx: Borrowed from Latin astronomus, from Ancient Greek ἀστρονόμος (astronómos)

verb:abnehmen.tx: From Middle High German abenëmen, from Old High German abanëman, from Proto-Germanic *abanemaną. Equivalent to ab- + nehmen. Cognate with Dutch afnemen.

noun:Ausschreitung.tx: From ausschreiten + -ung, initially in the sense of "stepping off the (proper) path".

noun:Auktionator.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin auctiōnātor, from auctiōnor (“I hold an auction”).

verb:akzeptieren.tx: Adapted borrowing of Latin acceptāre + -ieren. The Latin verb is a frequentative form of Latin accipere.

noun:Artikel.tx: From Middle High German artikel, from Latin articulus.

verb:anweisen.tx: From Middle High German anewīsen. Equivalent to an- + weisen.

noun:Anlass.tx: From Middle High German anelāȥ, anlāȥ. By surface analysis, deverbal from anlassen.

verb:abfinden.tx: From the Middle Low German verb and construct affinden. Equivalent to ab- + finden.

noun:Ausführung.tx: Derivative of ausführen (“to execute”) + -ung. Equivalent to Swedish utförande.

verb:ausführen.tx: From Middle High German ūȥvüeren, from Old High German ūȥfuoren. By surface analysis, aus (“out”) + führen (“to lead”). Compare Dutch uitvoeren.

noun:Aufenthalt.tx: From Middle High German ūfenthalt (“stay”), derived from ūfenthalten, a variant of ūfhalten, whence modern German aufhalten (“to stay”).

noun:Abiturient.tx: Borrowed from Latin abituriēns, present participle of abituriō (“to want to leave”).

noun:Andacht.tx: From Middle High German andāht, Old High German anadāht (“attention, devotion”).

adj:andächtig.tx: From Middle High German andæhtec, from Old High German anathāhtī. By surface analysis, Andacht + -ig.

verb:aufwenden.tx: From Middle High German ūfwenden (“to reach up(wards)”), from Old High German ūfwenten (“to erect”), from Proto-West Germanic *uppwandijan. Equivalent to auf- + wenden. The modern meaning emerged in the 15th century.

noun:Alman.tx: Borrowed from Turkish Alman (“German”), ultimately from French Allemand.

noun:Abwesenheit.tx: From abwesend + -heit. The elision of the d is regular; compare Unwissenheit, Zuvorkommenheit etc.

adj:abgeschmackt.tx: Alteration of earlier abgeschmack (with the same meaning). Equivalent to ab- + Geschmack (“taste”) + -t.

adj:äquivalent.tx: From Latin aequivalentem, accusative singular of aequivalēns, present active participle of aequivaleō (“to be equivalent, have equal power”).

noun:Äquivalent.tx: From Latin aequivalentem, accusative singular of aequivalēns, present active participle of aequivaleō (“to be equivalent, have equal power”).

noun:Ausgang.tx: From Middle High German ūzganc, from Old High German ūzgang (“exit, outgang”), from Proto-Germanic *ūtgangaz. Equivalent to aus- + Gang, also analyzable as deverbal from ausgehen. Cognate with Dutch uitgang (“exit”), English outgang (“egress, exit”). More at outgang.

adj:attraktiv.tx: Borrowed from French attractif, from Latin attractīvus.

adj:akzeptabel.tx: 17th century, from French acceptable. By surface analysis, akzeptieren + -abel.

adj:annehmbar.tx: Derived from the verb annehmen: annehm- (“accept”) + -bar (“-able”).

noun:Abschied.tx: From Middle High German abeschit, equivalent to ab- + Schied (“divorce, separation”). See also abscheiden (“to separate”).

noun:Anbau.tx: Back-formation from anbauen (“to cultivate”). Compare Luxembourgish Ubau.

verb:ankern.tx: From Middle High German ankern, synchronically analyzed as Anker + -n.

noun:Abzug.tx: Inherited from Middle High German abezuc, equivalent to ab- + Zug, semantically acting as a deverbal of abziehen.

verb:abziehen.tx: From Middle High German abeziehen, abziehen, from Old High German abaziohan, from Proto-West Germanic *abateuhan, from Proto-Germanic *abateuhaną; compare Middle Dutch aftien, Old Saxon aftiohan, Old English oftēon, Gothic 𐌰𐍆𐍄𐌹𐌿𐌷𐌰𐌽 (aftiuhan). By surface analysis, ab- + ziehen.

verb:anstecken.tx: From Middle High German anestecken, from Old High German anasteckōn. Equivalent to an- + stecken.

verb:auffallen.tx: From Middle High German ūfvallen, ūffallen, equivalent to auf- + fallen. Cognate with Middle Low German upvallen.

verb:aufnehmen.tx: From Middle High German ūfnëmen, from Old High German *ūfnëman, from Proto-West Germanic *uppneman. Equivalent to auf- + nehmen. Cognates include Dutch opnemen and Old English upniman.

noun:Angabe.tx: From angeben. Equivalent to an- + Gabe.

adj:allmählich.tx: From Middle High German almehlich. By surface analysis, all- + mählich (“slow”), from Proto-Germanic *makaz; related to Old Norse makligr.

adv:allmählich.tx: From Middle High German almehlich. By surface analysis, all- + mählich (“slow”), from Proto-Germanic *makaz; related to Old Norse makligr.

verb:ausweiden.tx: From Middle High German ūzweiden. Equivalent to aus- + weiden.

prep:angesichts.tx: From the genitive case of Angesicht, preserving the original sense of "viewing, sight".

noun:Ausland.tx: Back-formation from Ausländer (“foreigner”), from Middle High German ūzlender, from ūzlant (“outlying fields”), which had no continuation in Early New High German. By surface analysis, aus + Land. Compare English outland.

noun:Amin.tx: From English amine. By surface analysis, Am(moniak) + -in.

adj:abtrünnig.tx: From Middle High German abetrünnic, abetrünnec (also abetrünne), from Old High German abtrunnīg, abatrunnīg.

verb:antreiben.tx: By surface analysis, an- + treiben. Cognate with Luxembourgish andreiwen; Dutch aandrijven and Middle Dutch aendriven.

verb:abtreiben.tx: From Middle High German abetrīben, from Old High German abatrīben. Equivalent to ab- + treiben.

verb:abkupfern.tx: Appeared in 17th century, when engravers (German: Kupferstecher) were used large-scale to copy paintings and other works of art.

verb:annektieren.tx: Mid-19th century, from Latin annectere, semantically after English annex.

noun:Ausfahrt.tx: Deverbal from ausfahren, equivalent to aus- + Fahrt.

verb:auswerfen.tx: From Middle High German ūȥwërfen, from Old High German ūȥwërfan. Equivalent to aus- + werfen.

verb:anlaufen.tx: From Middle High German aneloufen, from Old High German analoufan, anahloufan. Equivalent to an- + laufen. Cognate with Dutch aanlopen.

noun:Aufstieg.tx: From Middle High German ūfstīc, from Old High German ūfstīg, from Proto-West Germanic *uppastigi (“ascension”). Cognate with German Low German Upstieg, Middle English upstiȝe, upsti, upstei.

noun:Abstieg.tx: Verbal noun of absteigen, derived from the past-tense grade stieg ab. Possibly attested as Middle High German abestic, if this has a short vowel (rather than more probable abestīc); compare also abesteic. Analysable as ab + Stieg.

noun:Augenärztin.tx: From Augenarzt (“eye doctor”) + -in or Auge (“eye”) + -n- (“doctor”) + Ärztin.

adv:abhanden.tx: Middle High German. By surface analysis, ab + Handen (now Händen).

verb:abstreifen.tx: From Middle High German abestreifen, from Old High German abastreifen, equivalent to ab- + streifen.

noun:Ausgabe.tx: From Middle High German ūȥgābe; related to geben (“to give”). Cognate with Luxembourgish Ausgab. Compare Dutch uitgave.

verb:ächten.tx: From Middle High German æhten, āhten, from Old High German āhten, from Proto-West Germanic *ą̄htijan. By surface analysis, Acht + -en.

verb:anstellen.tx: From Middle High German anestellen. Equivalent to an- + stellen.

num:anderthalb.tx: From Old High German andar halb, anderhalb (literally “second half”). Anderthalb is the single surviving relic of an older system to describe fractions, which counted from the higher ordinal number rather than the lower cardinal. Compare Old English ōþer healf, Dutch anderhalf, Danish halvanden. Compare also the use of the word halb in the sense of a half-hour before the following hour, such as …

verb:aalen.tx: The sense of to hunt eels derives from Aal (“eel”). The colloquial senses derive from the appearance of the eel and its way of moving.

verb:angehen.tx: From Middle High German anegān, from Old High German anagān. Equivalent to an- + gehen. Compare Dutch aangaan.

noun:Agoraphobie.tx: Borrowed from French agoraphobie, from Latin agoraphobia, from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá, “gathering of people or place of gathering”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

adj:anderer.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ander, from Old High German andar, from Proto-West Germanic *anþar. Cognate with Old Saxon ōthar (whence Low German anner), Old Dutch andar (whence Dutch ander), Old Frisian ōther (whence West Frisian oar), Old English ōþer (whence English other), Old Norse annarr (whence Swedish annan, Danish anden, Icelandic annar) and Yiddish אַנדער (ander).

pron:anderer.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ander, from Old High German andar, from Proto-West Germanic *anþar. Cognate with Old Saxon ōthar (whence Low German anner), Old Dutch andar (whence Dutch ander), Old Frisian ōther (whence West Frisian oar), Old English ōþer (whence English other), Old Norse annarr (whence Swedish annan, Danish anden, Icelandic annar) and Yiddish אַנדער (ander).

verb:abbeißen.tx: From Middle High German abebīzen, from Old High German ababīzan, equivalent to ab- (“off”) + beißen (“bite”).

noun:Abbruch.tx: From Middle High German abebruch. By surface analysis, deverbal from abbrechen.

verb:ausbilden.tx: From Middle High German ūzbilden. Equivalent to aus- + bilden.

noun:Anwesenheit.tx: From anwesend + -heit. The elision of the d is regular, compare Unwissenheit, Zuvorkommenheit etc.

verb:ausgeben.tx: From aus- + geben. Cognate with English outgive.

noun:Aue.tx: From Middle High German ouwe (“terrain, landscape by water, in water; island”), from Old High German ouwa, from Proto-West Germanic *auwju (“floodplain, meadow; island”), from Proto-Germanic *awjō, from earlier *agwjō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ékʷeh₂ (“water”). Compare with Old Frisian ei, Swedish ö, Danish ø, Old Norse ey, Norwegian øy; also related to the modern German suffix -ach.

adj:aufrichtig.tx: From Middle High German ūfrihtic. Equivalent to auf- (“up-”) + richtig (“correct, accurate, right”).

verb:ableiten.tx: From Middle High German abeleiten, from Old High German abaleiten. Equivalent to ab- + leiten. Cognate to Dutch afleiden.

verb:anwenden.tx: an + wenden. Compare Middle Low German anwenden.

noun:Anamnese.tx: From Late Latin anamnēsis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάμνησις (anámnēsis, “calling to mind, reminiscence”), from ἀνα- (ana-) + μιμνήσκω (mimnḗskō, “to remind, remember”).

noun:Abscheu.tx: From ab- + scheu. Compare Dutch afschuw, Swedish avsky, and Norwegian Bokmål avsky.

noun:Absage.tx: Back-formation from absagen. Attested earlier as Middle High German abesage, Old High German abasaga.

verb:aufrufen.tx: From auf + rufen (“to call, to shout”).

noun:Augenklappe.tx: From Auge + -n- + Klappe. Compare Yiddish אױגנקליאַפּע (oygnklyape), Dutch oogklep (“blinker, blinder”)

adj:abstrus.tx: Borrowed from Latin abstrūsus. The alternative meaning of "absurd" is likely a result of contamination from absurd itself, both often being used in similar contexts.

adv:abstrus.tx: Borrowed from Latin abstrūsus. The alternative meaning of "absurd" is likely a result of contamination from absurd itself, both often being used in similar contexts.

verb:aufhalten.tx: From Middle High German ūfhalten. Equivalent to auf- + halten. Cognates include Dutch ophouden and English uphold.

verb:aufkommen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ūfkomen, from Old High German ūfquëman. By surface analysis, auf- + kommen

adv:achtern.tx: From German Low German achtern (“in the back”) from achter (“behind”), from Middle Low German achter. Equivalent to Old High German aftero, cf. modern German After (“anus”). Cognate also to Dutch achter, achteren; English after. Borrowed to modern standard German only in the context of navigation (otherwise hinten).

noun:Anklage.tx: From Middle High German aneklage, from Old High German klaga. Compare Old Saxon klagon, Yiddish אָנקלאָג (onklog).

noun:Ampulle.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin ampulla. Doublet of Ampel

noun:Aufseher.tx: From Middle High German ūfseher. By surface analysis, agent noun of aufsehen in its obsolete meaning of oversee.

verb:abweisen.tx: From Middle High German abewīsen. Equivalent to ab- + weisen. Compare Dutch afwijzen, Low German afwiesen, West Frisian ôfwize.

noun:Alraune.tx: From Middle High German alrūne, from Old High German alrūna (“mandrake, sorceress”). Cognate with Gothic 𐍂𐌿𐌽𐌰 (rūna, “secret”).

verb:aufpassen.tx: auf- + passen, a calque of Dutch oppassen. The sense “to be attentive” is not borrowed from French (as is the verb stem passen) but a native development of Dutch.

adj:außerordentlich.tx: From außer (“outside; besides”) + ordentlich (“orderly”). Compare English extraordinary.

adv:außerordentlich.tx: From außer (“outside; besides”) + ordentlich (“orderly”). Compare English extraordinary.

noun:Auftragsmörder.tx: From Auftrag (“order, mission, contract”) + -s- (“interfix, Fugen-s (in German)”) + Mörder (“killer, hitman”).

noun:Anziehungskraft.tx: Anziehung 'attraction' from anziehen 'to attract' (from an- 'to(ward)' + ziehen 'to pull') + Kraft 'force, strength'

adj:artig.tx: From Middle High German ertec. Equivalent to Art + -ig.

noun:Abschaum.tx: Deverbal from abschäumen. Analyzable as ab- + Schaum.

verb:ausflippen.tx: Partial calque of English flip out.

noun:Ä.tx: * (letter) From Alemannic Middle High German aͤ, a representation of secondary umlaut [æ]. In Early Modern German, the letter spread to Central German, which did not have a special phoneme for secondary umlaut. Therefore, ä was seen there as a marker of umlaut as such, and was used analogously. * (sound) Middle High German distinguished up to five stressed e-vowels: [æ], [ɛ], [ɛː], [e], [eː]. …

verb:abwaschen.tx: From Middle High German abewaschen, from Old High German abawaskan. Equivalent to ab- + waschen.

verb:ausdrücken.tx: From Middle High German ūȥdrücken, equivalent to aus- (“out”) + drücken (“to press”). In the sense “to express” a calque of Latin exprimere. Compare Dutch uitdrukken.

noun:Aids.tx: Borrowed from English AIDS, from acquired immune deficiency syndrome.

noun:Aufstrich.tx: Deverbal from aufstreichen (“spread on, spread onto”).

verb:abbekommen.tx: From Middle High German abebekomen. Equivalent to ab- + bekommen.

verb:anstarren.tx: From Middle High German anestarren. Equivalent to an- + starren.

noun:Alzheimer.tx: A form of Altesheim (“old hamlet”) + -er; see altes and Heim.

noun:Ampfer.tx: From the equivalent Middle High German ampfer, Old High German ampfaro m, allied to the equivalent Old English ompre, from Proto-West Germanic *amprō; an adjective used as a substantive. Compare Dutch amper (“sharp, bitter, unripe”), Old Swedish amper, Old Norse apr (“sharp, chiefly of cold”) (for Proto-Germanic *ampraz); also Low German ampern (“to prove bitter to the taste”). Sauerampfer (also …

noun:Aspie.tx: Borrowed from English aspie, itself a derivation of German Asperger.

noun:Atze.tx: Attested since the end of the 18th century and originally probably from the Netherlands. While most likely a diminutive, it is unknown which given name Atze has developed out of; it likely emerged in different dialects independently. Candidates include Andreas, Artur and Matthias (whence Matze). The similar sounding diminutive Azo developed from Aldelbertus with Azzo being attested since 1259 in …

noun:Abriss.tx: Deverbal from abreißen. Equivalent to ab- + Riss.

noun:Abitur.tx: Attested since the 1890s. A shortening of Abiturium n, itself short for Latin exāmen abiturium—in formal German of the 19th century rather found as Abiturientenexamen—, from abituriō (“to wish to leave”), desiderative construction of abeō (“to leave, go off”). For more, see also Abiturient. Compare Physikum.

adj:angeboren.tx: From Middle High German angeborn, from Old High German anagiboran, from Proto-West Germanic *anagaboran. Equivalent to an- + geboren.

noun:Auflauf.tx: From Middle High German ūflouf. By surface analysis, deverbal from auflaufen.

noun:Alb.tx: From Middle High German alb, alp, from Old High German alp, from Proto-West Germanic *albi, from Proto-Germanic *albiz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós. Doublet of Elf, borrowed from English later.

noun:Amphore.tx: Borrowed from Latin amphora, from Ancient Greek ἀμφορεύς (amphoreús).

verb:abfallen.tx: From Middle High German abfallen, abvallen, abefallen, abevallen, abe vallen, equivalent to ab- + fallen. Cognate with German Low German offallen, Dutch afvallen, West Frisian ôffalle, Saterland Frisian oufale, oufaale, Middle English offallen (modern English fall off).

verb:ausgehen.tx: From Middle High German ūzgēn, ūzgān, from Old High German ūzgangan, ūzgān, ūzgēn, from Proto-West Germanic *ūtgān, equivalent to aus- + gehen. Cognate with German Low German utgahn, Dutch uitgaan, English outgo, Swedish utgå.

adj:achte.tx: From Middle High German ahtode, from Old High German ahtodo, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtudō. Equivalent to acht + -te.

verb:abführen.tx: From Middle High German abevüeren, from Old High German abafuoren. Equivalent to ab- + führen.

verb:ähneln.tx: 17th century, alteration of earlier ähnlichen, from Middle High German anelīchen, which is equivalent to ähnlich (“similar”) + -en. The contemporary form is possibly based on the association of ähnlich with the etymologically unrelated Ahn (“ancestor”), thus derived as Ahn + -eln; compare French s'apparenter à.

noun:Akelei.tx: From Middle High German ageleie, from Old High German ageleia, agaleia, agleia, acoleia, akileia (9ᵗʰ century) from the obscure Medieval Latin aquilegia which became translingual Aquilegia.

noun:Antisemitismus.tx: anti- + Semitismus, supposedly coined by Wilhelm Marr c. 1879-1885; see anti-Semitism for more.

verb:anklagen.tx: From Middle High German aneklagen. Equivalent to an- + klagen.

verb:aufgehen.tx: From Middle High German ūfgān, ūfgēn, from Old High German ūfgangan, ūfgān, ūfgēn. Equivalent to auf- + gehen. Compare Dutch opgaan.

verb:abhängen.tx: ab- + hängen. Likely a calque of Latin dependeo, in the informal sense a semantic loan from English hang out. Cognate Norwegian Bokmål avhenge.

noun:Arbeitszeug.tx: From Arbeit (“work”) + -s- + Zeug (“gear, equipment; clothing, clothes”).
